opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a pretty central thread for me, even if it wasn't always obvious from the outside. Back in grad school, a lot of my early work was about structured linear maps: matrices that can be represented and multiplied much more efficiently than a generic dense matrix. Think low-rank, sparse, Toeplitz, butterfly-type factorizations, and so on. The question was, what are the right primitives that are both expressive and computationally efficient?

When I moved into sequence modeling with HiPPO and then S4, that perspective carried over directly. A state space model is a linear dynamical system, and when you unroll it over a sequence, what you're really computing is a big structured matrix that maps inputs to outputs. Making these models practical came down to finding the right structure. In S4, that meant the diagonal-plus-low-rank parameterization and turning the whole thing into a convolution you could compute quickly. That's a structured matrix problem at heart.

With Mamba, and especially Mamba-2, it became even more explicit. The state space duality framework basically says that these selective SSMs and certain forms of attention are two ways of computing with the same class of structured matrices, semiseparable matrices. Once you see it that way, you get a nice unifying picture. Attention corresponds to one kind of structure, SSMs to another, and you can borrow algorithms and hardware-efficient tricks across the two.

So I'd say the structured matrix lens shaped my approach in two ways. First, it gives me a language for asking what a sequence model actually computes, separate from how it's implemented. Second, it keeps efficiency front and center. I don't think about expressivity in isolation; I'm always asking what structure lets us scale this to really long sequences and run it well on actual hardware. That interplay between math and systems is where I think a lot of the interesting progress happens.

r001.rationale: It says S4’s diagonal-plus-low-rank structure enabled a fast convolution, making the model practical.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling to very long sequences, but does not ask whether sequence models can handle potentially infinite context.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. It's funny, because when I started my PhD, structured matrices were really the thing I was working on, and sequence modeling wasn't even on my radar. The original motivation was really about efficiency in a general sense: dense matrix multiplies are the core primitive in deep learning, and the question was whether you could replace them with matrices that have some kind of structure, so that you get fewer parameters or faster compute, without losing expressivity. So I spent a long time thinking about things like low-rank, Toeplitz, butterfly matrices, and how to parameterize them and learn them.

What that did, I think, was change how I look at a model. I tend to see a model as a linear operator with some structure, plus a bit of nonlinearity, rather than as a stack of modules. And when you look at sequence models through that lens, a lot of things collapse into the same object. A convolution is a Toeplitz matrix. Attention is a data-dependent matrix. A recurrence is a particular factorization of a lower-triangular matrix. Once you see it that way, the question stops being "RNN versus transformer versus convolution" and becomes "what structure does the sequence mixing matrix have, and what does that structure buy you."

That's really where the state space line of work came from. The HiPPO stuff was about asking what matrix you'd want in a recurrence if you cared about remembering a long history, and the answer turned out to be a very specific structured matrix. Then S4 was almost entirely a structured matrix problem: the model was simple to write down, but computing it efficiently required diagonal-plus-low-rank structure and Cauchy kernels and all that. And with Mamba and the later work, the same thing shows up again. The reason you can make the recurrence selective and still train it fast is that the underlying operator is a semiseparable matrix, and there's this whole duality where you can compute the same thing as a recurrence or as a matmul depending on which structure you exploit.

So I'd say the biggest influence is that it gave me a vocabulary for tradeoffs. Every architecture is making a bet about structure, and structure is what determines what hardware you can run it on, how it scales with sequence length, and what it can actually represent. Having spent years staring at those matrices just makes those bets a lot more legible to me, and it's also been a pretty reliable way to find new models: look for a structure people haven't used yet, and ask what it would mean as a sequence model.

r001.rationale: The response says S4’s efficient computation relied on diagonal-plus-low-rank structure and Cauchy kernels.

r002.rationale: It discusses remembering a long history, but does not pose whether sequence models can handle potentially infinite context as a conceptual capability question.

astra-6.text:
A common thread in my research has been asking how we can impose structure on a computation to make it more efficient without losing the ability to model something interesting. With sequence modeling, that becomes a question of how you represent the past: what information do you keep, and how do you update that representation as new inputs arrive?

A state space model gives you a natural way to think about that. You have a hidden state that evolves over time, and a matrix controls how information is carried forward. But the structure of that matrix matters a lot. It affects both what the model can remember and how efficiently you can compute the updates.

So structured matrices gave me a way to connect those two questions. Instead of treating long-range memory and computational efficiency as separate problems, we can design the underlying dynamics with both in mind. That perspective has really shaped how I approach sequence modeling.

r001.rationale: It says structured matrices let the model’s dynamics be designed with computational efficiency in mind, clearly linking structure to efficient computation in the state space model discussion.

r002.rationale: It discusses representing and remembering the past, but does not pose whether sequence models can handle potentially infinite context as a capability question.

sol-6.1.text:
The connection, for me, is that a sequence model is doing a computation over a potentially very long history, and the structure of that computation matters a lot. If you use a completely general matrix, you have a lot of flexibility, but it can be expensive to compute with and difficult to understand what information the model preserves.

Structured matrices give you a way to make that tradeoff more deliberately. In a state space model, for example, you compress the history into a state that you update as new inputs arrive. The key question is what that update should look like so that the state retains useful information over long time scales. The matrix structure can help with both that memory problem and the efficiency of computing the updates.

So that work shaped my approach by getting me to think about the mathematical structure first: what computation do we want the model to perform, and how can we parameterize it so that it’s expressive, trainable, and efficient on long sequences?

r001.rationale: It says matrix structure helps make state-update computations efficient in a state space model, directly linking structured matrices to computational efficiency.

r002.rationale: It refers to a potentially very long history, but does not pose whether sequence models can handle potentially infinite context as a capability question.
